claim: ERK is activated by phosphorylation by a host of divergent extracellular signals.
source: However, because ERK is activated by phosphorylation by a host of divergent extracellular signals, more complex modes of regulation must exist in order to direct ERK activity toward appropriate responses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, drawing from the scientific consensus about ERK activation mechanisms.

claim: Different extracellular signals induce distinct temporal patterns of ERK activation to encode specific signaling information.
source: Previous studies have shown that different extracellular signals induce distinct temporal patterns of ERK activation to encode specific signaling information (Murphy et al., 2002; Herrero et al., 2016; Sasagawa et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: In PC12 cells, EGF treatment leads to transient ERK phosphorylation and cell proliferation.
source: For example, in model cell lines such as PC12 or MCF7, EGF treatment leads to transient ERK phosphorylation and cell proliferation, whereas alternate extracellular signals such as Nerve Growth Factor (NGF) or heregulin, respectively, induces sustained ERK phosphorylation and cell differentiation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous studies in the field.

claim: NGF induces sustained ERK phosphorylation and cell differentiation in PC12 cells.
source: For example, in model cell lines such as PC12 or MCF7, EGF treatment leads to transient ERK phosphorylation and cell proliferation, whereas alternate extracellular signals such as Nerve Growth Factor (NGF) or heregulin, respectively, induces sustained ERK phosphorylation and cell differentiation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous studies in the field.

claim: ERK substrates have been identified in many subcellular compartments including at the Golgi Apparatus.
source: ERK substrates have been identified in many subcellular compartments including at the Golgi Apparatus (Jesch et al., 2001; Shaul and Seger, 2006; Wainstein and Seger, 2016), at the mitochondrial membrane (Tomer et al., 2018; Nagdas et al., 2019), and near the plasma membrane (Mendoza et al., 2015; Mendoza et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: ERK substrates have been identified at the mitochondrial membrane.
source: ERK substrates have been identified in many subcellular compartments including at the Golgi Apparatus (Jesch et al., 2001; Shaul and Seger, 2006; Wainstein and Seger, 2016), at the mitochondrial membrane (Tomer et al., 2018; Nagdas et al., 2019), and near the plasma membrane (Mendoza et al., 2015; Mendoza et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: ERK substrates have been identified near the plasma membrane.
source: ERK substrates have been identified in many subcellular compartments including at the Golgi Apparatus (Jesch et al., 2001; Shaul and Seger, 2006; Wainstein and Seger, 2016), at the mitochondrial membrane (Tomer et al., 2018; Nagdas et al., 2019), and near the plasma membrane (Mendoza et al., 2015; Mendoza et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: EKAR4 was created by swapping the positions of ECFP and Ypet fluorescent proteins within the EKAR-EV biosensor.
source: In seeking to develop a new EKAR biosensor with sufficient dynamic range in order to maximize signal when the biosensor is restrained to specific locations, we found that switching the positions of the fluorescent proteins within the EKAR-EV biosensor such that Ypet was positioned C-terminally and ECFP was positioned N-terminally (Figure 1A) yielded a biosensor that generated an 74.5 ± 2.3% increase in the Y/C emission ratio in PC-12 cells (n = 83) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the biosensor response.

claim: EKAR4 generates a 74.5 ± 2.3% increase in the Y/C emission ratio in PC-12 cells.
source: In seeking to develop a new EKAR biosensor with sufficient dynamic range in order to maximize signal when the biosensor is restrained to specific locations, we found that switching the positions of the fluorescent proteins within the EKAR-EV biosensor such that Ypet was positioned C-terminally and ECFP was positioned N-terminally (Figure 1A) yielded a biosensor that generated an 74.5 ± 2.3% increase in the Y/C emission ratio in PC-12 cells (n = 83) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 83 cells.

claim: EKAR4 has a significantly improved dynamic range compared to EKAR2G1 and EKAR-EV in HEK-293 cells.
source: We also directly compared EKAR4 to EKAR2G1 and EKAR-EV in HEK-293 cells and observed a significantly improved dynamic range from the previous biosensors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the biosensors, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: EGF induces transient ERK activity in the cytosol.
source: EGF induced transient ERK activity in the cytosol and nucleus (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C), consistent with previous reports.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: EGF induces transient ERK activity in the nucleus.
source: EGF induced transient ERK activity in the cytosol and nucleus (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C), consistent with previous reports.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: EGF-stimulated pmEKAR4 response is much more sustained at the plasma membrane compared to cytosol and nucleus.
source: In contrast, EGF-stimulated pmEKAR4 response was much more sustained at the plasma membrane (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), compared to cytosol and nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: EKAR4 response at the plasma membrane is statistically different from the cytoplasmic and nuclear ERK responses.
source: Using this metric, we were able to determine that EKAR4 response at the plasma membrane was indeed statistically different from the cytoplasmic and nuclear ERK responses (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The kinetics of ERK activity accumulation are slower at the plasma membrane versus cytosol and nucleus.
source: Interestingly, we also found that the kinetics of ERK activity accumulation were slower at the plasma membrane versus cytosol and nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F), using the time to ½ maximum responses as a proxy (Bünemann et al., 2003; Ryu et al., 2015; Wan et al., 2019), which is dependent on both ERK and phosphatase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F and citations to methods.

claim: Addition of 10 µM SCH772984 at 10 min after EGF stimulation results in an immediate change in the slope of pmEKAR4 signal.
source: We found that addition of 10 µM SCH772984, but not of DMSO (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), either at 10 min after EGF stimulation (Figure 2A blue curve) or at 40 min post-stimulation (Figure 2A orange curve) resulted in an immediate change in the slope of pmEKAR4 signal, indicating that ERK was still actively phosphorylating pmEKAR4 at these time points (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of 10 µM SCH772984 at 40 min post-stimulation results in an immediate change in the slope of pmEKAR4 signal.
source: We found that addition of 10 µM SCH772984, but not of DMSO (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), either at 10 min after EGF stimulation (Figure 2A blue curve) or at 40 min post-stimulation (Figure 2A orange curve) resulted in an immediate change in the slope of pmEKAR4 signal, indicating that ERK was still actively phosphorylating pmEKAR4 at these time points (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ERK is still actively phosphorylating pmEKAR4 at 10 and 40 minutes after EGF stimulation.
source: We found that addition of 10 µM SCH772984, but not of DMSO (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), either at 10 min after EGF stimulation (Figure 2A blue curve) or at 40 min post-stimulation (Figure 2A orange curve) resulted in an immediate change in the slope of pmEKAR4 signal, indicating that ERK was still actively phosphorylating pmEKAR4 at these time points (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observation that ERK inhibitor addition causes immediate changes in biosensor signal.

claim: Addition of U0126 at 10 min or 40 min post EGF leads to decreases in the slope of pmEKAR4 signal.
source: Furthermore, addition of U0126, an inhibitor of the upstream kinase MEK, at 10 min or 40 min post EGF also led to decreases in the slope of pmEKAR4 signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating MEK was also active.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: MEK is active at 10 and 40 minutes after EGF stimulation.
source: Furthermore, addition of U0126, an inhibitor of the upstream kinase MEK, at 10 min or 40 min post EGF also led to decreases in the slope of pmEKAR4 signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating MEK was also active.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observation that MEK inhibitor addition causes changes in biosensor signal.

claim: ERK associated with the plasma membrane is equally phosphorylated between the 15- and 40 min time points after EGF treatment.
source: ERK was phosphorylated transiently in the cytoplasm and ERK associated with the plasma membrane was, on average, equally phosphorylated between the 15- and 40 min time points (Figure 2B, quantitated from five independent replicates in C), indicating the presence of a continuously phosphorylated pool of ERK at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical fractionation data shown in Figure 2B and quantified in Figure 2C from five independent replicates.

claim: ERK is phosphorylated transiently in the cytoplasm after EGF treatment.
source: ERK was phosphorylated transiently in the cytoplasm and ERK associated with the plasma membrane was, on average, equally phosphorylated between the 15- and 40 min time points (Figure 2B, quantitated from five independent replicates in C), indicating the presence of a continuously phosphorylated pool of ERK at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical fractionation data shown in Figure 2B and quantified in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a continuously phosphorylated pool of ERK at the plasma membrane.
source: ERK was phosphorylated transiently in the cytoplasm and ERK associated with the plasma membrane was, on average, equally phosphorylated between the 15- and 40 min time points (Figure 2B, quantitated from five independent replicates in C), indicating the presence of a continuously phosphorylated pool of ERK at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that plasma membrane ERK phosphorylation remains constant between 15 and 40 minutes.

claim: Rap1 can specifically interact with B-Raf and lead to sustained ERK activity under certain conditions.
source: However, it has been shown that Rap1, a GTPase in the Ras family, can in some cases specifically interact with B-Raf and lead to sustained ERK activity under certain conditions (Takahashi et al., 2017; Li et al., 2016; York et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: NGF-induced sustained ERK activation in PC12 cells is mediated through Rap1.
source: For example, NGF-induced sustained ERK activation in PC12 cells is mediated through Rap1 (York et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous published work.

claim: Ras activates a rapid and intense ERK response.
source: More recent reports suggest that while Ras activates a rapid and intense ERK response, Rap1 induces a slow and steady ERK response (Li et al., 2016), mimicking the observed kinetic difference between responses of pmEKAR4 and cytoEKAR4.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous published work.

claim: Rap1 induces a slow and steady ERK response.
source: More recent reports suggest that while Ras activates a rapid and intense ERK response, Rap1 induces a slow and steady ERK response (Li et al., 2016), mimicking the observed kinetic difference between responses of pmEKAR4 and cytoEKAR4.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous published work.

claim: Rap1 needs to be localized near the plasma membrane in order to activate the ERK pathway.
source: In addition, Wang et al. showed that in order for Rap1 to activate the ERK pathway, Rap1 needs to be localized near the plasma membrane (Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous published work.

claim: EGF induces activation of Rap1A in PC12 cells.
source: Using these biosensors in PC12 cells (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1B for diagram of pathway including inhibitors and biosensors utilized throughout this study), we observed that EGF consistently induced increases in Y/C emission ratios, indicating activation of both Rap1A (25.4 ± 4.7%, n = 11) and Rap1B (26 ± 3.4%, n = 8); this effect was completely abrogated by either co-expression of the Rap1-specific GTPase-activating protein Rap1GAP, which selectively inactivates Rap1 by inducing the hydrolysis of the bound GTP to GDP (Figure 3A,B, red curves, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Brinkmann et al., 2002; Chen et al., 1997), or by GGTI-298, a geranylgeranyltransferase I inhibitor that has been used to inhibit the processing, and thus action, of Rap1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Chenette and Der, 2011; Ke et al., 2019; McGuire et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 11 cells using Rap1A-FLARE biosensor.

claim: EGF induces activation of Rap1B in PC12 cells.
source: Using these biosensors in PC12 cells (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1B for diagram of pathway including inhibitors and biosensors utilized throughout this study), we observed that EGF consistently induced increases in Y/C emission ratios, indicating activation of both Rap1A (25.4 ± 4.7%, n = 11) and Rap1B (26 ± 3.4%, n = 8); this effect was completely abrogated by either co-expression of the Rap1-specific GTPase-activating protein Rap1GAP, which selectively inactivates Rap1 by inducing the hydrolysis of the bound GTP to GDP (Figure 3A,B, red curves, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Brinkmann et al., 2002; Chen et al., 1997), or by GGTI-298, a geranylgeranyltransferase I inhibitor that has been used to inhibit the processing, and thus action, of Rap1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Chenette and Der, 2011; Ke et al., 2019; McGuire et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 8 cells using Rap1B-FLARE biosensor.

claim: Co-expression of Rap1GAP completely abrogates EGF-induced Rap1A and Rap1B activation.
source: Using these biosensors in PC12 cells (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1B for diagram of pathway including inhibitors and biosensors utilized throughout this study), we observed that EGF consistently induced increases in Y/C emission ratios, indicating activation of both Rap1A (25.4 ± 4.7%, n = 11) and Rap1B (26 ± 3.4%, n = 8); this effect was completely abrogated by either co-expression of the Rap1-specific GTPase-activating protein Rap1GAP, which selectively inactivates Rap1 by inducing the hydrolysis of the bound GTP to GDP (Figure 3A,B, red curves, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Brinkmann et al., 2002; Chen et al., 1997), or by GGTI-298, a geranylgeranyltransferase I inhibitor that has been used to inhibit the processing, and thus action, of Rap1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Chenette and Der, 2011; Ke et al., 2019; McGuire et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: GGTI-298 completely abrogates EGF-induced Rap1A and Rap1B activation.
source: Using these biosensors in PC12 cells (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1B for diagram of pathway including inhibitors and biosensors utilized throughout this study), we observed that EGF consistently induced increases in Y/C emission ratios, indicating activation of both Rap1A (25.4 ± 4.7%, n = 11) and Rap1B (26 ± 3.4%, n = 8); this effect was completely abrogated by either co-expression of the Rap1-specific GTPase-activating protein Rap1GAP, which selectively inactivates Rap1 by inducing the hydrolysis of the bound GTP to GDP (Figure 3A,B, red curves, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Brinkmann et al., 2002; Chen et al., 1997), or by GGTI-298, a geranylgeranyltransferase I inhibitor that has been used to inhibit the processing, and thus action, of Rap1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Chenette and Der, 2011; Ke et al., 2019; McGuire et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: EGF induces an average maximum response of 64.8 ± 11% increase in ratio of EGFP to mCherry at the basal membrane in TIRF microscopy assays.
source: In these cells, EGF induced an average maximum response of 64.8 ± 11% (n = 11) increase in ratio of EGFP to mCherry at the basal membrane, while control cells expressing EGFP showed no changes in EGFP fluorescence intensity at the membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 11 cells using TIRF microscopy.

claim: Co-expression of Rap1GAP abolishes the translocation of RBD to the membrane.
source: Furthermore, co-expression of Rap1GAP abolished the translocation of the RBD, further confirming the specificity of the response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Rap1GAP expression significantly dampens pmEKAR4 response.
source: Having verified EGF induces Rap1 activation near the plasma membrane, we investigated how abrogation of Rap1 would affect plasma membrane localized ERK activity. We used several different approaches to inhibit Rap1. First, Rap1GAP-mediated inhibition of both Rap1A and Rap1B led to a dramatic dampening of EGF-induced ERK activity near the plasma membrane (Figure 3C,E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Rap1GAP has no effect on cytosolic ERK activity.
source: However, Rap1GAP had no effect on cytosolic ERK activity (Figure 3D,F), indicating that the effect of Rap1GAP is plasma membrane specific.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D,F.

claim: The effect of Rap1GAP is plasma membrane specific.
source: However, Rap1GAP had no effect on cytosolic ERK activity (Figure 3D,F), indicating that the effect of Rap1GAP is plasma membrane specific.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Rap1GAP affects plasma membrane but not cytosolic ERK activity.

claim: Rap1B N17 dramatically decreases Rap1B activation.
source: Secondly, we expressed Rap1A and Rap1B dominant-negative isoforms (Rap1A N17 and Rap1B N17) (Maly et al., 1994). While Rap1A N17 was not able to inhibit Rap1A activation, Rap1B N17 dramatically decreased Rap1B activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B,D) and led to a similar effect on pmEKAR response as Rap1GAP expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 5F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B,D.

claim: Rap1B N17 leads to a similar effect on pmEKAR response as Rap1GAP expression.
source: Secondly, we expressed Rap1A and Rap1B dominant-negative isoforms (Rap1A N17 and Rap1B N17) (Maly et al., 1994). While Rap1A N17 was not able to inhibit Rap1A activation, Rap1B N17 dramatically decreased Rap1B activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B,D) and led to a similar effect on pmEKAR response as Rap1GAP expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 5F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5F,G.

claim: Acute Rap1A inhibition by GGTI-298 results in a drastically decreased pmEKAR4 response.
source: In addition, acute Rap1A inhibition by GGTI-298 also resulted in a drastically decreased pmEKAR4 response (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Rap1 is critically involved in regulating plasma membrane ERK activity.
source: These data indicate that Rap1 is critically involved in regulating plasma membrane ERK activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing that Rap1 inhibition reduces plasma membrane ERK activity.

claim: Rap1 inhibition does not completely abrogate plasma membrane ERK response.
source: However, we note that Rap1 inhibition does not completely abrogate plasma membrane ERK response.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the experimental data showing residual ERK activity after Rap1 inhibition.

claim: HRas-N17 completely abolishes cytosolic ERK activity.
source: We thus used HRas-N17, a dominant negative form of H-Ras that inhibits all Ras isoforms (Matallanas et al., 2003), to probe how inhibition of Ras affects both cytosolic and plasma membrane localized ERK. We found that cytosolic ERK activity was completely abolished (Figure 3—figure supplement 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6A,B.

claim: HRas-N17 alters but does not abolish plasma membrane localized ERK activity.
source: We also found that plasma membrane localized ERK activity was altered, but not abolished like the cytoEKAR4 response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the effects of HRas-N17 on plasma membrane versus cytosolic ERK.

claim: The amplitude of pmEKAR4 at 40 min is not different between HRas-N17 expressing cells and control cells.
source: Interestingly, the amplitude of pmEKAR4 at 40 min was not different between HRas-N17 expressing cells and control cells, indicating that Rap1, not Ras, is responsible for plasma membrane ERK activity at later time points.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6E.

claim: Rap1, not Ras, is responsible for plasma membrane ERK activity at later time points.
source: Interestingly, the amplitude of pmEKAR4 at 40 min was not different between HRas-N17 expressing cells and control cells, indicating that Rap1, not Ras, is responsible for plasma membrane ERK activity at later time points.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that HRas-N17 does not affect late-phase plasma membrane ERK activity.

claim: Plasma membrane targeted EMBer significantly reduces ERK activity near the plasma membrane.
source: Using plasma membrane targeted EMBer tagged with mCherry (pmEMBer), we observed a significantly reduced ERK activity near the plasma membrane (Figure 4A) but not in the cytosol (Figure 4B) or nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Plasma membrane targeted EMBer does not reduce ERK activity in the cytosol.
source: Using plasma membrane targeted EMBer tagged with mCherry (pmEMBer), we observed a significantly reduced ERK activity near the plasma membrane (Figure 4A) but not in the cytosol (Figure 4B) or nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Plasma membrane targeted EMBer does not reduce ERK activity in the nucleus.
source: Using plasma membrane targeted EMBer tagged with mCherry (pmEMBer), we observed a significantly reduced ERK activity near the plasma membrane (Figure 4A) but not in the cytosol (Figure 4B) or nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In cells expressing pmEMBer, there is an apparent change in cell morphology from primarily circular to primarily elliptical.
source: In cells expressing pmEMBer, we first observed an apparent change in cell morphology from primarily circular to primarily elliptical (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual observations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In cells without pmEMBer, 58% of imaged cells have a minor:major axes ratio greater than 0.8.
source: In cells without pmEMBer, 58% of imaged cells have a minor:major axes ratio greater than 0.8, indicating that the majority of cells were nearly perfectly round.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative morphology analysis data.

claim: 42% of pmEMBer expressing cells have a minor:major axes ratio below 0.6.
source: In contrast, 42% of pmEMBer expressing cells had a ratio below 0.6.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative morphology analysis data.

claim: ERK activity near the membrane has an important role in controlling cell morphology.
source: This drastic change in cell morphology, which is dependent on pmEMBer expression at the plasma membrane, indicates that ERK activity near the membrane has an important role in controlling cell morphology.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that pmEMBer expression changes cell morphology.

claim: In normal conditions, 28% of cells have protrusions longer than 5 µm.
source: Specifically, in normal conditions, 28% of cells had protrusions longer than 5 µm and the protrusions of 25% of these cells lasted for longer than 15 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of protrusion dynamics data.

claim: In normal conditions, 25% of cells have protrusions lasting longer than 15 min.
source: Specifically, in normal conditions, 28% of cells had protrusions longer than 5 µm and the protrusions of 25% of these cells lasted for longer than 15 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of protrusion dynamics data.

claim: In pmERK-inhibited conditions, 70% of cells have protrusions longer than 5 µm.
source: In contrast, in plasma mebrane ERK (pmERK)-inhibited conditions, 70% of cells had protrusions longer than 5 µm and 75% of pmERK-inhibited cells had protrusions lasting longer than 15 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of protrusion dynamics data.

claim: In pmERK-inhibited conditions, 75% of cells have protrusions lasting longer than 15 min.
source: In contrast, in plasma mebrane ERK (pmERK)-inhibited conditions, 70% of cells had protrusions longer than 5 µm and 75% of pmERK-inhibited cells had protrusions lasting longer than 15 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of protrusion dynamics data.

claim: Rac1 is a known substrate for ERK.
source: Importantly, Rac1 is a known substrate for ERK, and EGF-induced Rac1 phosphorylation by ERK in COS-7 cells was shown to lead to inhibition of Rac1 and its removal from the plasma membrane (Tong et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous published work.

claim: EGF-induced Rac1 phosphorylation by ERK in COS-7 cells leads to inhibition of Rac1 and its removal from the plasma membrane.
source: Importantly, Rac1 is a known substrate for ERK, and EGF-induced Rac1 phosphorylation by ERK in COS-7 cells was shown to lead to inhibition of Rac1 and its removal from the plasma membrane (Tong et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous published work.

claim: A robust 6.4 ± 0.7% increase in Rac1-2G response to EGF is observed under pmERK-inhibited conditions.
source: Although we could not observe RhoA activity under either condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D,E), using Rac1-2G we did observe a robust 6.4 ± 0.7% increase in response to EGF (n = 19, control; n = 24, with pmEMBer) under pmERK-inhibited conditions but not under control conditions (Figure 4E,F), indicating endogenous pmERK inhibits Rac1 activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 24 cells with pmEMBer shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: No Rac1-2G response to EGF is observed under control conditions.
source: Although we could not observe RhoA activity under either condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D,E), using Rac1-2G we did observe a robust 6.4 ± 0.7% increase in response to EGF (n = 19, control; n = 24, with pmEMBer) under pmERK-inhibited conditions but not under control conditions (Figure 4E,F), indicating endogenous pmERK inhibits Rac1 activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 19 control cells shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Endogenous pmERK inhibits Rac1 activation.
source: Although we could not observe RhoA activity under either condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D,E), using Rac1-2G we did observe a robust 6.4 ± 0.7% increase in response to EGF (n = 19, control; n = 24, with pmEMBer) under pmERK-inhibited conditions but not under control conditions (Figure 4E,F), indicating endogenous pmERK inhibits Rac1 activation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Rac1 activation is only observed when plasma membrane ERK is inhibited.

claim: Plasma membrane ERK activity inhibits Rac1, which could contribute to the regulation of membrane protrusion dynamics.
source: This observation is consistent with previous reports in which ERK phosphorylation of Rac1 on T108 inhibits Rac1 and leads to relocalization of Rac1 away from the membrane (Tong et al., 2013) and indicates that plasma membrane ERK activity inhibits Rac1, which could contribute to the regulation of membrane protrusion dynamics.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: EGF simultaneously activates at least three divergent sub-populations of ERK with unique temporal dynamics: the cytosol, the plasma membrane, and the nucleus.
source: In this study, we established the use of fluorescent, FRET-based biosensors to study the spatiotemporal dynamics of ERK activity by targeting the biosensors to specific subcellular regions, particularly the plasma membrane, cytosol, and nucleus. Using this technique, we discovered that EGF simultaneously activates at least three divergent sub-populations of ERK with unique temporal dynamics from each other: the cytosol (Figure 1C), the Plasma membrane (Figure 1D), and the nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The nuclear EKAR4 response exhibits the most transient of the targeted EKAR4 biosensors.
source: Indeed, the nuclear EKAR4 response exhibits the most transient of the targeted EKAR4 biosensors, followed by cytoEKAR4, with the pmEKAR4 exhibiting an apparent persistent response (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The sustained pmEKAR4 signal is a direct result of continued ERK phosphorylation of the biosensor.
source: By using a membrane-permeable ERK inhibitor, we confirmed that the sustained pmEKAR4 signal was a direct result of continued ERK phosphorylation of the biosensor and not because the biosensor was unable to be dephosphorylated by a lack of phosphatases near the membrane (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observation that ERK inhibitor addition causes immediate changes in biosensor signal.

claim: EGF does activate Rap1 at the plasma membrane in PC12 cells.
source: In this study, with the use of recently reported Rap1 biosensors (Figure 3A–B; O'Shaughnessy et al., 2019) and our live-cell TIRF-based EGFP-RalGDS translocation assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), we were able to show that, in PC12 cells, EGF does indeed activate Rap1 at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using Rap1 biosensors and TIRF microscopy.

claim: Rap1 is critically involved in regulating plasma membrane ERK activity but does not appear to contribute to the Ras-dependent cytosolic or nuclear ERK activities.
source: Using Rap1GAP (Figure 3C–F), a dominant negative form of Rap1B (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), and the geranylgeranyl transferase I inhibitor (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), combined with our plasma membrane ERK activity reporter, we further showed that Rap1 is critically involved in regulating plasma membrane ERK activity but does not appear to contribute to the Ras-dependent cytosolic or nuclear ERK activities, whereas Ras appears to primarily contribute to the initial, but not sustained, component of plasma membrane ERK activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Ras appears to primarily contribute to the initial, but not sustained, component of plasma membrane ERK activity.
source: Using Rap1GAP (Figure 3C–F), a dominant negative form of Rap1B (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), and the geranylgeranyl transferase I inhibitor (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), combined with our plasma membrane ERK activity reporter, we further showed that Rap1 is critically involved in regulating plasma membrane ERK activity but does not appear to contribute to the Ras-dependent cytosolic or nuclear ERK activities, whereas Ras appears to primarily contribute to the initial, but not sustained, component of plasma membrane ERK activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Inhibition of membrane-localized ERK activity potentiates EGF-induced Rac1 activation.
source: Furthermore, our study provides a striking example where an individual extracellular signal, such as EGF, can temporally regulate subcellular ERK populations to control distinct cellular processes. We showed that inhibition of membrane-localized ERK activity potentiates EGF-induced Rac1 activation and leads to enhanced membrane protrusion dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased Rac1 activation when plasma membrane ERK is inhibited.

claim: Inhibition of membrane-localized ERK activity leads to enhanced membrane protrusion dynamics.
source: Furthermore, our study provides a striking example where an individual extracellular signal, such as EGF, can temporally regulate subcellular ERK populations to control distinct cellular processes. We showed that inhibition of membrane-localized ERK activity potentiates EGF-induced Rac1 activation and leads to enhanced membrane protrusion dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in protrusion dynamics when plasma membrane ERK is inhibited.
